Okay. Look, the numbers are good. I'm not going to pretend they're not. When I showed our CEO the on-time number he was happy, for about a week. And then the twenty-fourth happened, and that's what he remembers now. So.

It started a little after seven our time, which is the first wave, that's the busiest hour we have. Drivers are loaded and out. And the ETAs just stopped moving. The app kept showing times, so nobody on our side knew anything was wrong, the times just weren't real. And our customer texts go out off those ETAs. So about eleven hundred customers got a delivery window that was wrong. Some by twenty minutes, some by over an hour. And grocery customers, you know, they're waiting at home for frozen stuff, they planned their morning around it. Our support line got absolutely hammered. And honestly, the outage itself, things break, I've run operations long enough, I get it. The part that I'm actually upset about is that we heard about it from our drivers. Not from you. A driver called Aisha and said the app was frozen, and that was the first anyone at Brightside knew. And then your status page said everything was green for, what was it, twenty-six minutes? I had my team refreshing it. Green. So I'm on the phone with my support lead telling her I don't know what's happening, and your page is telling me nothing is happening.

Yeah, it was — so the drivers have a group chat, and by like seven-twenty it was just everyone posting screenshots. Is anyone else's app stuck. Restarting phones. A couple of them started calling customers directly from their personal phones to give them a real time, which, I appreciate the hustle, but we really don't want drivers doing that while they're driving. And I couldn't tell them anything because I didn't know anything. I ended up telling everyone to ignore the app times and just run the stop order, which, that's basically going back to paper.

And then the comps. We comped delivery fees on, I want to say three hundred-something orders, where the window was off by more than an hour or the frozen stuff was soft when it got there. That's our cost, we made that call, I'm not asking you to eat it line by line. But I want you to understand it wasn't just an annoying morning.
No, that's — thank you for laying it out. That's more detail than I had, honestly. I knew it was bad, I didn't know about the comps.

Yeah. So first, I'm sorry. And I want to be specific about what I'm sorry for, because I think you're right about where the real failure was. The ETA service went down for forty-seven minutes, and that's bad, but the part that's genuinely on us and shouldn't have happened is that you found out from your drivers, and that our status page sat green for twenty-six minutes. That's not a technical limitation. Our status page is updated by hand right now, and during the incident the person running it was also the person debugging it. That's a process failure and it's mine to fix, not your problem to work around.
Okay. I appreciate you saying that.

And just quickly on what actually happened, so you've got it. We had a failover in one of our Redis clusters, that's a cache that sits behind the ETA service. That on its own should be a blip. But our dispatch workers started retrying all at once, no backoff, no randomness, so they basically hammered the ETA service until it fell over. And the cached ETAs your drivers were seeing were stale, and nothing in the app told them that. We did a full retro last Friday, the day after. Coming out of it, the workers get proper retry budgets with jitter, the ETA service gets a circuit breaker so it degrades instead of collapsing, and the status page gets updated automatically from our alerts, so a human doesn't have to remember to do it in the middle of a fire. We're also adding a staleness flag, so if an ETA is old, the driver app says so instead of showing a confident wrong number.
Why did it take you that long to even know? Twenty-six minutes, I mean, my drivers knew in five.

Honestly, our alerting was too lenient. The threshold was set so it only paged once errors had been high for a sustained window, which is meant to stop false alarms at three in the morning, but it meant our on-call engineer got paged about six minutes after it started instead of right away. And then it took a while to figure out that the cache failover was the cause and not the symptom. Those thresholds are being tightened this week. That's not an excuse, it's just the honest answer to why.

The staleness flag, yeah. That's actually the one I care about most for the drivers. If it had just said ETA updating or something, they would have known. They wouldn't have been restarting phones for twenty minutes.

Fine. What I'd add is, the status page being automatic is good, but I don't want to be checking a status page. If something hits our fleet, I want a call or a text. Me and Aisha. Before our drivers know.

Yes. That's — I'm writing a customer comms runbook right now, that came out of the retro too, and part of it is exactly that. For accounts like yours there's a named contact list and a pre-approved message we send within, the target is fifteen minutes. I'll add you and Aisha by text, today. And I'll send you the written incident report by Friday, so you have something to hand to your CEO that isn't just me saying sorry on a call.
That would help. He's going to ask me for it.

And then, look, I have to ask. We had nine hundred support calls and eleven hundred customers with bad windows. Some of those we comped. I need to go back with something. What are we talking about on a service credit?

It's meant to say we take it seriously.

And I'd rather you hold us to the second part than the credit, honestly. If there's another incident and you hear about it from a driver before you hear from Sofia, that's the thing I want you to call me about.
Okay. Let's move on before I get worked up again.

When someone gets a delivery window of nine to eleven, and it's ten-forty and nothing's showed up, they call us. If they had a link, half those calls go away. That's real money for my support team. And frankly, on the twenty-fourth, if they'd had a live link, at least they'd have seen the van moving.

Yeah. Let me give you the straight version, because I think you've gotten the soft version a couple of times and that's not fair to you. Live ETA sharing is not built. We haven't started it. We've scoped it, it's about five engineer-weeks of work, so it's not a giant project, but it's not nothing. And for Q4 it's competing directly with something else on our list, which is a redesign of the driver app onboarding, which, Aisha, I want to come back to with you, because I think it's relevant to you too. We're finalizing Q4 planning this week. Friday, actually.
Okay, but I've heard, we're figuring out Q4, before. In June it was, we're figuring out Q3.

That's fair. So here's what I'll commit to. By October ninth, so a week from Friday, I will send you the Q4 roadmap, and it'll have a date for live ETA sharing in it. A date, not a quarter. And if the honest answer is that the date is later than you want, I'll tell you that, and I'll tell you why, rather than giving you something vague and letting you find out in January.
A date. If I can't give you one I'll tell you exactly what it depends on, but I'm planning to give you one.
Okay. I'll hold you to that.

Please do. And I'll say one more thing on it, which ties back to the outage. If we'd shipped live ETA in July and then had the twenty-fourth, your customers would have been watching a live link show them a wrong time with total confidence. So the staleness work we're doing, the flag that says this ETA is old, that actually has to land before or with live ETA. It's not a reason to delay. It's just part of doing it right.

What does it actually look like, though? Like if I'm a customer. Do I get a text with a link, do I need to download something? Because if it's an app download, nobody's doing that for groceries.

Branded as Brightside, not as us. Your customers would never see the word Tandem. Right now when someone's anxious about their order they call the store, the store calls dispatch, dispatch calls the driver. A link would take a lot of that away.

And is it just us asking for this? Because if it's just Brightside, I get that it's harder to prioritize.

Sure. That's fine. Just make sure the date's actually in it.

Okay, so Aisha, that's actually a good handoff to you. Asher mentioned the driver onboarding work, and I know you've had some things you wanted to raise about the driver app. I'd love to just hear it, unfiltered.

The problem is new drivers, and specifically seasonal drivers. We staff up every year from mid-November through New Year's, Thanksgiving is our biggest week by a mile, and this year we're bringing on about forty-five seasonal drivers across the three metros. A lot of them have never driven for a delivery company. Some of them are, you know, college kids home for the holidays, some are retirees picking up shifts. And the first day with the app is rough.
Can you walk me through where it goes wrong? Like literally step by step, if you can.

Sure. So step one is login. Right now it's an email plus a company code. Our seasonal folks don't get a Brightside email, so they use their personal one, and half of them mistype it when we set them up, or they use a different one when they log in, and then they're locked out on their first morning, standing in the depot at six a.m., and a dispatcher has to stop what they're doing to sort it out. That alone, last November, I think we had something like a dozen lockouts in the first week.

Then permissions. Especially on Android. The phone asks, do you want to allow location all the time, only while using the app, or don't allow. And a new driver doesn't know what that means, so they tap only while using, because that sounds safer. And then they switch over to make a phone call or open the camera for a proof of delivery photo, and tracking just stops, and on our dispatch screen the van looks like it's parked for twenty minutes. And then dispatch calls them to ask if they're okay. Which, again, phone ringing while driving.
Yeah, we've seen that one on a couple of other accounts too.

And then the big one is the first route is real. There's no practice. Their first ever stop in the app is a real customer with real groceries. So they don't know how to mark a stop as customer not home, they don't know how to do a substitution note, they don't know that you can swipe to see the next three stops. And they panic a little, and they slow down, and they call dispatch. The experienced drivers end up training them in the parking lot, which, that's half a day of a good driver not driving.
What about proof of delivery? Is the photo step a problem, or is that one okay?

It's okay once they find it. The problem is it's two taps deep, so new people complete the stop without the photo, and then they get flagged, and then we get a dispute from the customer three days later saying their bags never showed up and we have no photo. That's maybe a smaller thing. But it's the same pattern, it's stuff that's obvious to someone who's done two hundred routes and invisible to someone on their first.
Yeah. Okay. I'm writing that one down, I don't think it's in the redesign yet.
And they quit. That's the part that costs me. We spend money recruiting them, we do the background check, and then they have one bad morning and don't come back.

Yeah. Last year we onboarded thirty-two seasonal drivers, and I think eleven of them never finished their first route. Or quit within the first, no, sorry, it was twelve. Twelve didn't make it through the first week. Some of that is just seasonal work, people flake. But a lot of it is that first morning.

Okay, so this is really helpful, and it lines up almost exactly with what we're seeing across all our customers. Across the board, about thirty-eight percent of new drivers drop off before they complete their first route. Our goal for Q4 is to get that below fifteen. Priya, who leads design on our side, has a redesign of the onboarding flow, and the three main pieces are basically your list. Login by phone number with a text code instead of email plus company code. A short permissions primer, three screens, that explains in plain language why the app needs location all the time before the phone asks the scary question. And a practice route, so a new driver can run through five fake stops in the depot, including a customer not home and a substitution, before they ever touch a real order.
Oh, okay. Yeah. That's — honestly, if you'd asked me to write the list, that's the list.

So my ask would be, would you be open to having a few of your drivers test it with Priya? Ideally new ones. Even four or five people. She'd do it in person or over video, half an hour each, and it'd be on the prototype, so nothing touches your live routes.

Yes. Absolutely. We have an early cohort of seasonal hires starting the third week of October, before the big wave. I could probably get you four or five of them. And I'll send over what I've got from last year too, I have a spreadsheet of the support tickets and the stuff dispatchers wrote down, it's messy but it's real.
Messy and real is perfect. I'll connect you and Priya this week.

Can I just, I want to make sure I understand. Earlier you said live ETA and this onboarding work are competing for the same people in Q4. So if you do this, are you telling me you're not doing live ETA?

It's a fair question. It's not quite either-or, but it is a real trade-off, and I'd rather be honest about it than pretend we have infinite engineers. Both of them pull on the same mobile and frontend folks. We're also hiring for exactly that right now, two senior frontend engineers, but realistically those people don't help us in Q4. I'll be honest, I want both.
I mean, for me, in November, onboarding matters more. If I lose twelve drivers in Thanksgiving week again, a tracking link doesn't help anybody, because the groceries aren't on a van.
No, it's genuinely useful for us to hear both of those, because they're both real. And it's good input for Friday.
Okay. Point taken. I still want both. But point taken.

If we have another twenty-fourth, especially in Thanksgiving week, I can't go to my CEO and say let's put another sixty vans on the same platform. I just can't. And two is live ETA. Sacramento is a new market for us, we're going to be competing with people who already have tracking links, and I'm not launching a new metro without one. So if the date you send me on the ninth is, I don't know, next summer, then I have to look at whether we run Sacramento on something else. I don't want to. But I would.
That's clear. And honestly, I appreciate you telling us straight instead of us finding out in December.

I'd rather tell you now. You've been good partners for two years. The numbers this quarter are proof of that. I'm not looking for an excuse to leave. I'm telling you what I need to be able to stay and grow.
And on reliability, what do I actually tell my CEO? Like, beyond the things you listed from the retro. Because he's going to say, how do you know it won't happen again in Thanksgiving week.

Two things you can tell him. One, we're going to start deliberately failing over that cache cluster every month, in a controlled way, so we find out how the system reacts on a Tuesday afternoon that we picked, not on a busy morning that we didn't. And two, we're going to put a change freeze around Thanksgiving week, no risky deploys to the dispatch or ETA paths that week. I can't promise you nothing will ever break. Nobody honest can. But I can promise that if it does, it breaks smaller, and you hear from us first.
Okay. The freeze, I like. Put that in writing in the incident report, if you can.

I'll put it in. And Aisha, on that, it'd help us to have your Thanksgiving week volume forecast. Orders per day, and how many vans you're running per metro. If we know the peak, we can make sure we're watching the right things that week.
Yeah, I can get you that. It's usually about one point six times a normal week, but I'll get the real forecast from planning. They do it by metro.

And if Sacramento's on the new onboarding flow from the start, that's sixty vans' worth of brand new drivers. That would be the best test you could ask for, honestly.
That's a really good point. Yeah.

turns: Hey Elena. Hi. Is Marcus on his way?

Hi Elena. Nice to meet you. Thanks for sending the export sample, by the way. That was really useful. I have a few questions about some of the columns, but we can get to that.
I assumed you would. Some of those columns, nobody knows what they mean. I'll answer what I can.
Ha. That's honest. There's one called ATTR_17 that I'm pretty sure is a dock door number, but it's also sometimes the word NONE, so.
It is a dock door. Sometimes. Yes.
Hey, sorry, sorry. I'm here. One of the Spokane trucks lost a mirror on a gate post this morning and I had to go look at it, which, I don't know why I had to go look at it, but I did.

Driver's fine. The gate post is not fine. Anyway. It's starting, peak's starting, everything's a little bit on fire. How are you guys?
Good, good. Busy week. I drove up to Vancouver yesterday for a customer and it took me an hour to get across the bridge, so I feel your pain on everything being on fire. It's the season.
Oh, the I-5 bridge at five o'clock? That's a choice. My drivers would tell you to go around on 205, but honestly that's not much better.
Ha. Next time. Okay. So, Marcus, this is Daniel, staff engineer. Daniel, Marcus runs operations.
Hey Marcus. Good to meet you.
Hey Daniel. Tom says you're the one who's going to tell me the truth.
I'll try. That's sort of my whole job on these calls.

Ha. Okay, so just a super quick recap so Daniel has the same picture. On Tuesday we talked about 420 trucks across three terminals, routes built in spreadsheets every night, overtime at about fourteen percent of driver hours, and around forty k a month in chargebacks. Elena walked us through Samsara and the Oracle TMS, and the integration being a gate, not a score. And we're working toward a decision by October 30th with Dana. Elena, I sent the SOC 2 report Wednesday, did that come through okay?
It came through. I'm reading it. I have some questions about the exceptions section, but I'll put them in writing.

Perfect. And we've got your questionnaire, the team's working through it. So, today, Daniel's going to show Routing v3 on your Kent data, the dispatch board, constraints, and what happens when a truck goes down. Then we'll go deep on Samsara and the TMS, and then I want to talk about what a pilot looks like. Daniel, take it away.
Cool. Let me share. Can everyone see a map with a lot of colored lines on it?

Okay. So this is the dispatch board. What you're looking at is Kent, last Tuesday, the actual orders from the export Elena sent, a hundred and thirty-eight trucks and just under fourteen hundred stops. Each color is a truck. On the left you've got the route list, one row per truck, with the driver, number of stops, total miles, and the projected end of day. Over here on the right, red means something's at risk, like a stop that's projected to miss its appointment window, or a driver who's going to run tight on hours. And I want to be upfront: I built this plan from the TMS export and the Samsara data, I did not have your dispatchers' tribal knowledge, so there's going to be stuff in here that's wrong in ways only Ray would know.
Ray would have opinions. Yeah. How many reds are there?

Right now, eleven. Mostly two DCs in Sumner where the appointment windows were really tight. And honestly, I'd guess your dispatchers already know those. For comparison, when I took the routes your team actually ran that night and scored them the same way, it was thirty-one reds, and about nine percent more miles. But again, salt. I'm comparing a plan to a plan, not to what actually happened on the road.
No, that's fair. Thirty-one feels about right, honestly. Tuesday was a bad night.

So let me show constraints, because that's usually where these things fall apart. If I click into a driver, say this guy, truck 2214. You can see his hours-of-service clock. That's coming straight from Samsara, so it's his actual remaining drive time and on-duty time, not an estimate. The solver treats that as a hard constraint. It will not build a route that puts him over, period. If the only way to cover a stop is to break someone's hours, it leaves the stop unassigned and flags it for a human.
Okay, wait. That's a big one. So it would rather leave a stop on the table than blow someone's hours.

Yes. By default. You can configure how much overtime you're willing to spend before it does that, like, allow up to an hour of overtime per driver if it saves a late delivery at a priority customer. But hours of service itself, the federal limit, is never negotiable in the solver.
Huh. Okay. I like that it asks a person instead of just quietly doing the dumb thing.

Then dock windows. So every stop has its appointment window from the TMS, but you can also set location rules. This is the part I think Ray will care about. Say this DC in Sumner, everyone knows dock wait is forty-five minutes on Tuesday mornings. You can set that here, service time forty-five minutes, Tuesdays, six to ten. And then every route that touches it accounts for it. You set it once and it sticks, instead of living in someone's head.
Where does that data live? The location rules. Is that in your system or does it need to go back into the TMS?
In ours. We don't write back to the TMS, at least not in what I'm proposing. That's a good question though, I'll come back to it in the integration part.

And then over time, the ETA model learns dock waits on its own from the Samsara geofences. That's Kenji's model, our ML engineer. It's gone from about six minutes of average error down to a bit over four this year. I'll be honest that dock wait time is still the hardest part for it, so for a while the manual rules are going to beat the model at your worst DCs. That's sort of why we let you override it.
Daniel, show them the lock thing.

Yeah. So, Marcus, you said on Tuesday, or Tom told me you said, that dispatchers want to override. So, a dispatcher can drag a stop from one truck to another, like this, and the board re-scores it instantly. If they like a route, they lock it, this padlock, and the solver will never touch it again. Everything else re-plans around the locked routes. So it's not all or nothing.
Can you lock part of a route? Like, these first three stops are sacred because the driver has a relationship with the receiver, but do whatever you want after?
Yes. You can lock a sequence. That's actually a common one. Grocery fleets do it all the time for their morning stores.
Okay. That's good. That's actually really good.

So now the fun part. Let's say it's 9:40 in the morning, and truck 2231 breaks down. Fuel pump, whatever. He's in Auburn, he's got eight stops left. So I'm going to mark the truck down. Right-click, out of service. And what happens now is the solver re-plans every unlocked route in the terminal, with everybody's current positions from Samsara, their remaining hours, and all the remaining windows. That's about four hundred stops still open at this point in the day. And, there. Done.

That's it. About four seconds for four hundred stops. It's in the corner there, 4.1 seconds. And you can see what it did. It split his eight stops across three trucks. Two of them were already nearby. And the one it flagged, this yellow one, is a driver who'll end up about twenty minutes into overtime, so it's asking the dispatcher, do you approve this or not. The dispatcher hits accept, and the new stops push to the drivers.

Okay. So, that's — I mean, today that's forty-five minutes of my lead on the phone. Minimum. And he'd probably have ended up giving all eight stops to one guy, because that's one phone call instead of three.
And that one guy is your overtime.

And that one guy is my overtime. Yeah. Okay. I'm just thinking out loud here. The part I'm trying to picture is what Ray does when he disagrees with it. Like, it splits the stops across three trucks, and Ray looks at it and goes, no, that driver's slow on residential, or that guy's truck doesn't have a liftgate. What does he do?

Two things. In the moment, he just drags the stop where he wants it and locks it, and the solver re-plans around his decision. Takes a second. And then longer term, the liftgate thing, that's a vehicle attribute. You tag the truck as no liftgate, you tag the stop as needs liftgate, and the solver never makes that mistake again. Driver preferences we can do too, but I'd start with the hard stuff like equipment.
Okay. That's the answer I wanted. If Ray feels like he's the boss of it, he'll use it.
Daniel, can you show the end-of-day view too? I think that's the screen Dana's going to care about.

Rate limits? We already have two internal dashboards hitting that API.

Option two is a middleware connector. In parallel, if the pilot looks good, we start the middleware connector so it's ready for the full rollout. I would not try to do the connector before the pilot. It'll eat your whole decision window.

Ten percent of sixty trucks is, what, call it sixty stops a day? Seventy? Ray already re-keys more than that. That's not the thing that kills this.
For the pilot. For 420 trucks it is the thing that kills it. So the connector has to be real, not a slide.

Agreed. And I'm not going to tell you we have one sitting on a shelf for your exact version. We've done this pattern for two other on-prem TMS installs, neither of them Oracle. I can share the architecture doc for one of those this week so you can see what you'd be approving.

One more thing, and I'm sorry, Tom, I know this is a sales call. You had an outage last week. Thursday. Your ETA service was down for, I think, forty-seven minutes. I read your status page.
No, that's fair. Daniel, do you want to take that?

Completely fair. That's the exact feedback we're taking from it.

Okay. So let me switch to the commercial side for a few minutes, because I know we're working back from October 30th. Our list price for Routing v3 is sixty-eight dollars per truck per month. Okay. Look, I'm not trying to beat you up on price on this call. I just need you to know the number's in the room. If the pilot's great, I can sell sixty-two. If it's fine, I'm going to lose that argument to fifty-two.

Ugh, now you're asking me to commit. Um. Okay, I'm thinking out loud. Put that in and I'll tell you if she flinches.

Sure. So, okay, the short version is we run 420 trucks. Mostly regional freight, LTL and some full truckload, Washington, Oregon, a little bit of Idaho. It's Excel, it's a handful of really smart people who have been doing it for fifteen years, and a lot of tribal knowledge about which dock at which DC is going to make you wait two hours if you show up at 6:05 instead of 5:55.
Right. How many people are building routes?

Nine dispatchers across the three terminals, plus two leads. And they start around, I want to say four in the afternoon, once the order cutoff hits, and on a bad night they're there till ten, eleven. Which, you know, they're salaried, so that's not my overtime number, but it's a burnout number. I lost a lead in Spokane in June and it took me three months to backfill.
Sorry, quick one. Roughly how many stops does a truck do in a day? Just so I have the shape of it in my head.

Depends on the terminal. Kent and Portland, the LTL trucks, eight to fourteen stops, a lot of them are DCs and some industrial. Spokane is longer hauls, fewer stops, more miles. If you averaged it out across the whole fleet, call it ten stops a truck. So something like four thousand stops a night, give or take, across the three terminals. On a peak day more.

And the thing is, they're good. Like, the routes aren't terrible. But they're built for the plan, right? And the plan's dead by 7 a.m. A truck goes down, a driver calls out, a DC pushes an appointment, and then it's phones and whiteboards and somebody re-sorting a spreadsheet at a stoplight. Not literally. Hopefully.
When a truck goes down mid-day, what actually happens? Like, who re-plans, and how?

The lead at that terminal. Mostly by gut. They'll pull up Samsara, look at who's closest, and call around. Hey, can you pick up these four stops on your way back. And the driver says yes, because they're nice people and they want the hours, and then they blow through their day, and that's my overtime problem.
Yeah, let's talk about that. What's overtime looking like?
So, it's — I literally had this number up this morning. It's about fourteen percent of driver hours. Fourteen, fifteen. Let's say fourteen, I'll get yelled at by finance if I round up.
Fourteen percent of total driver hours is overtime.

Of total hours, yeah. And our target internally, the number we actually budget for, is six. So we're more than double. And some of that's peak, sure, but it was eleven in the spring. It's not just a seasonal thing, it's been creeping for a year and a half.
And that's paid at time and a half, I assume.

Time and a half, yeah. And then there's the hours-of-service piece, which is the scarier one. If a driver hits their limit, we've got a truck sitting at a truck stop somewhere with somebody else's freight on it and a relief driver two hours away. That's happened. Twice in August.
Three times. Thank you. Elena keeps me honest. She has the Samsara logs, I have my memory.
Ha. Okay. And then on the customer side, you mentioned DCs. I'm guessing there are chargebacks?

Oh, yeah. That's the one that gets Dana's attention. So most of our big shippers, the retail ones, they run on-time-in-full programs. You miss your appointment window at the DC, they fine you. It's a percentage of the invoice or a flat fee depending on the retailer, and some of them are, honestly, pretty aggressive about it. There's one big-box account where fifteen minutes late is the same as not showing up. We're running about forty thousand a month in late-delivery chargebacks right now.

Give or take. Some months it's thirty-five. September was worse, I haven't seen the final yet. And that's money that just disappears. There's no fighting most of them, we've tried, the retailers have all the leverage.
Do you have a sense of how much of that is the plan being bad versus things going wrong during the day?

That's a great question and the honest answer is no, not really. My gut says it's like half and half. Some of it is we just build a route that was never going to make a 6 a.m. window at a DC, because the dispatcher forgot that dock is always backed up on Tuesdays, or they stacked too many stops before it. And some of it is the truck broke down at nine and nobody re-planned fast enough, so the 2 p.m. appointment at the other end of the route just quietly dies.
Okay. That's helpful. That split matters a lot for what we'd actually try to fix first. The nightly plan is the easier win, the mid-day re-plan is where it gets interesting.

So if I play that back. 420 trucks, three terminals, routes built manually every night in spreadsheets, overtime at fourteen percent of driver hours against a target of six, and about forty k a month in chargebacks. Plus the hours-of-service risk, which is more of a safety and compliance thing. Did I miss anything?
No, that's — when you say it out loud it's kind of bleak. There's one more, the customer calls, but let's park that. Elena's going to want to talk about systems before I get on my soapbox.
Ha. Fair. Let's park it, I wrote it down. What would good look like for you, though? Like, if we're sitting here in six months and this worked, what's different?

Honestly? Dispatchers go home at seven. Overtime under eight percent. Chargebacks cut in half, so call it twenty k a month instead of forty. If I could walk into Dana's office with that, I don't have to sell anything internally. It sells itself.
That's a really clear bar. I like that a lot. It's measurable, too, which makes my life easier. Have you tried to fix this before? Like, is there a routing tool that came and went?

Ha. Yes. So about four years ago, before my time actually, they bought a routing add-on that came bundled with the TMS. Oracle had a module. It ran overnight, it spat out routes, and the dispatchers looked at them and said these are garbage, and went back to Excel within like a month. And to be fair to the dispatchers, the routes were garbage. It didn't know anything about dock times, it didn't know a driver's hours, it just did shortest path. So there's a little bit of scar tissue on the floor. When I say routing software to my leads, the first face they make is not a happy face.
That's really good to know. So adoption with the dispatchers is its own thing we'd need to earn.
A hundred percent. If my Kent lead, Ray, doesn't buy in, it doesn't matter what I sign. He'll just quietly keep the spreadsheet open on his second monitor. I would, too, honestly, if I were him.

That's actually one of the things we designed around. Dispatchers can override anything the engine does, drag a stop, lock a route, and it'll re-plan around what they locked instead of fighting them. It's meant to feel like a really fast assistant, not an autopilot. But again, better to show than tell. Thursday or whenever we do the demo, it'd be great if Ray could be on.
Maybe. Let me see. He's not a big Zoom guy. But if I can get him to watch the recording, that might be enough.
Elena, over to you. What does the landscape look like on your side?

Okay. So, telematics is Samsara. All 420 trucks have Samsara units, we've been on them about three years. That part is fine, it's modern, there's an API, we already pull GPS and hours of service from it into a couple of internal dashboards. The problem is the TMS. We're on Oracle Transportation Management, on-prem, and the version is from 2014. It's heavily customized. Nobody who customized it still works here.

Yes. Very classic. So the orders live there. Customer appointments live there. Rates live there. And there is no real API. There are some database views that I'm allowed to read, and there's a batch export that runs every night for finance. That's it. Upgrading it is a separate project, and that project is not funded, so please don't tell me the answer is upgrade the TMS.
Ha, noted. Do the dispatchers export from the TMS into the spreadsheets today?
Yes. Every afternoon, the export lands on a shared drive, someone pastes it into the template. Sometimes the wrong day's file. That has also happened.
We don't talk about that week.

Okay, so, I won't pretend to be the right person for the deep integration question. That's exactly why I want Daniel on the next call. He's our staff engineer, he's built most of our integrations. But at a high level, we already have a Samsara integration, it's live with a number of our customers. And for the TMS side we've done file-based integrations before, so it's not a new problem for us.

Uh, that's a — I'd want to check which ones are specifically Oracle. I know we've done older on-prem TMS setups, there's a parcel fleet in Ohio on some ancient system, I don't remember which one off the top of my head. I'll get you a straight answer on that instead of guessing.
Please. Because I have heard 'we've done file-based integrations' from three vendors now and every time it turns out to be a CSV upload button in the UI and a person whose job is to click it.

That's fair. And for what it's worth, there's a real difference between someone uploading a CSV once a day and a scheduled pull with validation and error handling and alerting when the file doesn't show up. Daniel can walk you through what it actually looks like. I'd rather he show you than we describe it.
Okay. Good. I'll also want to know what happens when an order changes in the TMS after the export. Because that happens constantly.
Yeah, that's a good one. Is the change rate high? Like, how many orders get modified after the nightly cutoff?
I don't have a precise number. Marcus?

Ten percent? Maybe more in peak. Appointment changes mostly. A DC calls and moves a slot, or a customer adds a pallet. The dispatchers find out by phone and then somebody updates the TMS later. Sometimes much later.

So the TMS is not always the source of truth, is what he's saying. Which is a problem for any integration, not just yours. I just want to be clear about it up front so nobody acts surprised in the pilot.
No, that's really helpful. And on the network side, can anything talk to that box from the outside, or is it locked down?

Got it. So outbound SFTP is possible today, inbound is a change board. That's a good thing for Daniel to know before Thursday, or, sorry, before the demo, whenever we land it. Okay. Writing all that down. What else is on your list? Security, SSO?

Yes. So, SSO is Okta. Anything new has to be behind Okta, no exceptions, our CISO is very clear about that. SAML is fine. SCIM for provisioning would be nice, it's not a hard requirement. Then security review. I'll need your SOC 2 report, Type II, and we have a security questionnaire. It's, I think, about 180 questions. I'm sorry in advance.
No, that's totally normal. We're SOC 2 Type II, I can get you the report under NDA this week. And the questionnaire, send it over, we have folks who turn those around.

And roles. We'd need at least three. Dispatchers, terminal leads, and a read-only role for customer service. We manage all of that in Okta groups, so I'd want the roles to come from the group, not be set by hand in your admin screen by whoever remembers to do it.

Yep, we map roles from SAML group claims, so that works the way you'd want. I'll double check on SCIM, I believe it's supported on the enterprise plan, but I'd rather confirm than say yes and be wrong.
Okay. And the questionnaire, how long does it usually take you?
Usually about a week, a week and a half for one that size.
Hm. Okay. If it's a week and a half that's fine. If it's a month, that's the decision date, so.
No, understood. We'll prioritize it. I'll make sure it doesn't become the long pole.
Okay. And data. Where is the data hosted, and does any of our customer data go to third parties? Like, are you sending our stops to some mapping provider?

That'll all be in the questionnaire answers and the subprocessor list, but I want you to hear it now and not be surprised by it later.
Okay. I appreciate that. That's the kind of thing that usually comes up in week five.
Elena's killed two vendors in week five.
Ha. Noted. We'll try very hard not to be the third.

October 30th. We want a decision by the end of October. Dana does the budget for next year in November, and if it's not in by then, it's basically next fiscal year, and I really don't want to go through another peak like this one.
Okay, October 30. That's tight with a pilot in there, but doable if we move this week.
It's tight, I know. I'd rather it be tight.

Just thinking out loud. If the decision is October 30, the pilot can't be a full quarter. We'd need something that shows real signal in, what, four weeks? Can you get Dana a read on overtime in four weeks?

And budget, I'll just ask directly. Is there budget set aside for this, or is this something that has to be carved out?

If you come in and the pilot shows we save half the overtime and half the chargebacks, that's well over three hundred, and it's an easy conversation. Yeah. And look, I'll be straight with you about the other thing too, since you're going to ask anyway. We're talking to RouteWise.
Sure. I figured you might be.

If that holds on your fleet, a few dollars a truck is kind of a rounding error.
If it holds. Everybody's beta is great.

Forty k a month in chargebacks is call it four hundred and eighty k a year. If we take half of that, that's two-forty. Then overtime. I don't know your payroll, but if you've got, what, four-hundred-some drivers and fourteen percent of their hours are at time and a half, going from fourteen to eight is a big number. Probably bigger than the chargebacks. So against three hundred k, the math works pretty fast, even if we only hit half of what you said good looks like.

Live ETA sharing, tracking link, whatever you call it.

Yep, understood. That's a really good constraint to know now.

Use it. Please. Make the case. I'd rather you build it than RouteWise does.

The provider's saying a host failure on their side, the replica gets promoted, and from Redis's point of view that took about eleven seconds, which, that's fine, that's what failover is supposed to do. Fourteen fourteen, so two minutes later, the dispatch workers start throwing errors talking to the ETA service and start retrying. No backoff, no jitter, so they're all retrying on basically the same beat. That's the retry storm. ETA service starts falling over somewhere around fourteen fifteen, fourteen sixteen. Fourteen twenty, I get paged. Which is six minutes after the storm starts, and eight after the failover. I'll come back to why. Fourteen thirty-one, we've got a strong suspicion it's the Redis client not picking up the new primary, Daniel spotted that. Fourteen thirty-eight, status page goes up. That's twenty-six minutes after the start. Fourteen fifty-two, we throttle the workers and restart the ETA service's Redis client with a topology refresh. Fourteen fifty-nine, error rates back to baseline, ETAs flowing. So forty-seven minutes end to end, and three hundred and twelve fleets affected.
Can I add one thing to the timeline? There's a gap between thirty-one and fifty-two that I think matters.

So at around fourteen forty-one we tried just restarting the ETA service pods. On their own. Thinking, fresh process, fresh connections, it'll pick up the new topology. And it did come up, but the workers were still hammering it, so within two minutes it was falling over again. That's when we realized we had to throttle the workers first and then bring the service back. So the order of operations cost us probably ten minutes.
Right, yeah, I'll put that in. Fourteen forty-one, restart attempt, fourteen forty-three, it falls over again. Thanks.
Sorry, just to check, the three hundred and twelve, is that every fleet that had a route active at the time, or the ones that actually saw bad ETAs?

Good question. It's fleets that had at least one active route and made ETA calls during the window. So it's the ones that were actually touched, not everyone. Realistically almost all of them saw stale ETAs at some point, because of the caching thing Kenji's going to talk about.
Anyone have anything else on the timeline before we move on? Maya, you were in the channel from about fourteen twenty-five, right?

Yeah, about then. I don't think I have anything to add on the timeline itself. It matches what I saw. Maybe just, between twenty and thirty-one, what were you looking at? Because that's eleven minutes, and I think that's worth understanding.

Yeah, fair, and that's a bit embarrassing, but that's the point of this. When I got paged, the first thing I saw was the ETA service error rate, and there had been a deploy to the ETA service at thirteen fifty. So my brain went straight to, it's the deploy. And I spent, I think, five or six minutes diffing that deploy and getting ready to roll it back. It was a logging change. Totally harmless. Then Daniel joined and said, have you looked at Redis, and that's what turned it around.

And to be fair, the Redis dashboard looked healthy. That's what made it confusing. The cluster had already healed itself, so if you looked at Redis, Redis said I'm fine. It was only the client logs in the ETA service that showed it was still talking to the old primary.
Okay, so the signal was there, it was just in a place nobody would look first.
Yeah. Exactly that. I'll add the deploy red herring to the timeline, fourteen twenty to about fourteen twenty-six.

Okay, root cause. And I want to say upfront, I don't think there's one root cause here. I think there's a failover, which is a normal event that's going to happen again, and then three things that turned a normal event into a forty-seven minute outage. Daniel, do you want to take the Redis client part, since you found it?

Sure. So the client library we use in the ETA service keeps a local map of which node owns which slots in the cluster. When the primary fails over, the cluster knows about it within seconds, but our client doesn't, because periodic topology refresh is off by default in the library and we never turned it on. So it keeps sending requests to the old primary's address. And it gets errors back, or timeouts, and it doesn't go, oh, the topology changed, let me re-fetch it. It just reports the error upward. So from the ETA service's point of view, Redis is just broken. Indefinitely. Until the process restarts.
And we didn't hit this in the failover we had in, what was it, May?

We did, actually, but in staging. That's where the runbook came from. I wrote down the topology refresh fix at the time, and I filed a ticket to turn on refresh in prod config, and it, uh, it's still in the backlog. It got deprioritized behind Routing v3 stuff. Which, I'm not blaming anyone, I deprioritized it myself, I thought staging was a weird edge case.

Yeah, and I think that's worth writing down as a finding on its own, not to blame anybody, but because it's a pattern. We found the bug, we wrote the fix down, and the fix didn't make it to prod because there was no forcing function.
Can I ask a dumb question? It was one shard. Why did one shard failing over take out everything, instead of, like, a third of the requests?

Not dumb at all. It's because of how the ETA calls work. When a worker sequences a route, it asks for ETAs for every stop on the route, and those keys are spread across all the shards. So basically every single route touches the broken shard at least once. One shard broken means pretty much every request has at least one failing piece, and the way the code is written, one failing piece fails the whole request.
Got it. So it's not one third, it's all or nothing.
Pretty much. Which is another thing we could look at later, partial results, but that's a bigger change and I don't think it's a Q4 thing.
And just so it's clear, the model service doesn't touch that Redis cluster at all. It has its own feature store. So that's why it kept working.
Okay so that's one. Two is the retry behavior in the dispatch workers. Daniel, that's also kind of yours.

Yeah. So the dispatch workers call the ETA service for every stop they're sequencing. When a call fails, they retry, fixed two hundred milliseconds, up to five times, and then the whole job gets re-queued and starts over. No exponential backoff, no jitter, and no budget, meaning there's nothing that says, across this worker, if more than ten percent of my calls are retries, stop retrying. So when the ETA service started erroring, every worker, and we were running about eighteen hundred at that time of day, was retrying in lockstep. We roughly six-x'd the request rate on the ETA service in about ninety seconds. That's what actually knocked it over. Redis being broken made it error, the retries made it die.
Six-x is about what I saw on the gateway graphs too. It's a pretty dramatic spike, it's like a wall.

Yeah. And then three, which is mine. The ETA service has no circuit breaker. So when Redis started failing, instead of the service saying, okay, my dependency is down, I'm going to fail fast or serve something degraded and stop taking on more work, it just kept accepting requests and holding connections open waiting for Redis timeouts. Connection pool exhausted, threads stuck, health checks start failing, Kubernetes restarts the pods, they come back into the same storm, crash loop. If we'd had a breaker, I think the realistic version of this is ten or fifteen minutes of degraded ETAs, not forty-seven minutes of the service being down.
So if I'm summarizing, the failover was the trigger, but any one of those three, topology refresh, retry budget, circuit breaker, would have made this much smaller.
Yeah, that's how I'd put it. Any one of them. And we had none of them.
Is there a reason we didn't have a breaker? Like was that a decision or just never came up?

Honestly, never came up. The ETA service was a pretty thin layer when we built it, it was mostly a cache in front of Kenji's model, and nobody thought of it as a thing that could take the whole dispatch path down. It grew into being critical without anybody re-reviewing it. Which, again, I think is a pattern we should name.

One more on root cause. I think we should also say, the workers retrying the whole job on failure, not just the call, that amplified it too. A job that has forty stops, if call thirty-eight fails five times, the job re-queues and makes thirty-seven successful calls again. So it's not just retries, it's retries of retries. I'll fold that into the retry budget work, but I want it on the doc.

Okay, detection and comms. This is the part I'm least happy about, personally. So, the page. Our alert on the ETA service fires when the error rate is above ten percent for five consecutive minutes. That five-minute window is there because last year we had a lot of flappy alerts waking people up for blips. But the effect here is that the service was clearly broken from about fourteen fifteen, and I didn't get paged until fourteen twenty. So we were six minutes late on the storm and eight minutes late on the actual trigger.
Is there an alert on worker retry rate? That seems like the earliest signal.
There isn't. And, related, there's no alert on the Redis client side either, only on the cluster. So the cluster said healthy, the client was broken, and we only alert on the cluster.
And was secondary on-call ever paged? I didn't see Daniel get paged, I think he just saw the channel.
Yeah, I wasn't paged. I saw Ravi post in the channel and jumped in.

Right, secondary only gets paged if primary doesn't acknowledge within fifteen minutes. I acked in one minute, so it never escalated. That ties to what I'm going to say about the status page.

But back to Maya's question. Retry rate is on my list. That, and the gateway request rate, because a six-x spike in ninety seconds should be screaming. I'd like to tighten the error threshold to something like a two-minute window with a higher threshold, and add the retry rate alert. I'll look at the last three months of data so we don't just go back to the flappy alerts.

I didn't think about it until Maya asked in the channel whether we'd posted anything.
I only asked because Sofia had pinged me, to be fair.
Yeah, so can I talk about what this looked like from the customer side? Because I think this is the part that's going to hurt us the most, more than the forty-seven minutes.

And that's — every customer I've talked to since, that's the thing. Not that it broke. That we didn't tell them.
Yeah. That's the part I'm worried about for the QBR next week too.
Right, the Brightside QBR is Wednesday. And I'm going to have to sit across from Jordan and explain why the status page was green. And I'd rather explain what we're changing than just apologize.

Yeah. That's fair. And I'll own that. I think the fix is that a human shouldn't be updating it at all in the first minutes. If a sev-one alert fires, the status page should go to investigating automatically, with a generic message, and then a human refines it. Better to have a slightly vague yellow banner at fourteen twenty than a perfect message at fourteen thirty-eight.
Plus one. And honestly, separate the roles. The IC shouldn't be the person debugging. We're small, but we had four engineers in the channel. One of us could have been on comms.
Yeah. That's fair too. I grabbed both because I was first in. I'll put that in the incident process.

And from my side, the status page being automatic is necessary but it's not enough. Our biggest accounts, they don't watch a status page. Jordan wants a phone call. So I need a comms runbook. Who on the CS side gets pulled in, at what severity, which accounts get a direct call or text, and, honestly the big one, pre-approved message templates. Because yesterday, even once I knew what was going on, I spent fifteen minutes wordsmithing an email and then waiting for someone to tell me if I was allowed to say Redis.
Ha. You're allowed to say Redis.

Good to know! But that's my point, I shouldn't have to ask mid-incident. If there's a template that says, we're seeing degraded ETAs, here's what your drivers should do, next update in thirty minutes, and it's already been approved, I can send it in two minutes. I'll write it. I just want everyone here to know it's coming and to review the templates, especially the technical bits.
That's great. Put me down as a reviewer. And I'd love for the status page automation and your runbook to fire off the same trigger, so they're not two separate things someone has to remember.
Okay. Kenji, you wanted to talk about the ETA side specifically, because I think there's a piece here that isn't in my timeline at all.

Yeah. So, first, just so it's in the doc, the model service was fine the whole time. I checked it at, like, fourteen twenty-four when I joined the channel. Latency normal, prediction volume dropped because nobody could reach it, but nothing wrong with the model or the service. So that's not part of the root cause.
Yep, and that was actually helpful, it took one thing off the table early.

Right. But the thing I want to flag is what customers actually saw. Because the ETA service going down didn't make ETAs disappear. It made them stale. Two places. The driver app holds the last ETA it got for each stop and just keeps counting down from it. So a driver who's stuck at a dock for twenty minutes, the app is still saying, arriving in four minutes, arriving in three. And then the notification service, which sends the customer delivery window texts, it reads from the ETA snapshot table. That table stopped getting updated at about fourteen fourteen, but the notification service kept reading it and kept sending windows off it. Nothing anywhere in the chain knew the number was old. So for up to about forty-five minutes we were sending customers confident, precise, wrong times.
Which is exactly what Brightside saw. That's the eleven — sorry, they're saying over a thousand of their customers got wrong windows. They haven't given me an exact number yet.
Over a thousand from one fleet?

One fleet. Their morning wave is huge, it's grocery, seven a.m. is peak for them. And their support line got swamped. Across everyone, we got forty-one tickets, twenty-three different fleets. But Brightside was by far the worst because of the timing.

And the driver side was rough too. Aisha told me their drivers were in a group chat posting screenshots, restarting their phones, and a few of them started calling customers from their personal phones to give a real time. Which she does not want drivers doing while they're driving. So the stale number didn't just mislead customers, it made drivers think the app was broken on their end.
Which, to be fair, it kind of was.
It kind of was! But they couldn't tell the difference between their phone being broken and our whole system being down. That's the thing.

Yeah, and that's the part that bugs me most, honestly, as the person who owns the ETA numbers. We spent all year getting the error down from six point one minutes to four point three, and then for forty-five minutes on Thursday the error was, like, unbounded, and we were showing it with the same confidence as a good prediction. Accuracy doesn't matter much if we can't tell people when we don't know.

So my proposal is a staleness flag. Every ETA we produce carries a computed-at timestamp. It technically already has one internally, we just don't expose it. Every consumer checks it. If it's older than some threshold, I'd start with five minutes, the ETA is marked stale. In the driver app, instead of a countdown it says ETA updating. In the notification service, we hold the customer text instead of sending a stale window. On the dispatcher dashboard we gray it out. It's not glamorous, but it changes the failure mode from wrong to honest.
Is five minutes right for everyone though? Like for dense urban routes the ETA moves a lot in five minutes. For rural freight five minutes is nothing.

Yeah, fair. I'd make it configurable per fleet, default five. Honestly, dense urban is already where the model struggles most, so for those fleets you might even want shorter. I don't want to overthink it for v1 though. Any flag is a big improvement over no flag.

Can I push on one thing? Holding the customer text. I get why, but from the customer side, getting nothing is also bad. If you're expecting a window and the text just doesn't come, you call support, and then we're back to the support line getting hammered.
Yeah, that's fair. I was thinking of it from the, don't send wrong data angle.

Right, and I agree with that. But maybe instead of holding it, if it's stale, the notification service sends a fallback, like, your delivery is running a little behind schedule, we'll text you an updated window shortly. Oh, I like that better. Okay, so stale means fallback message, not no message. I'll write it up that way. And the fleets can override the wording, I assume? Brightside's going to want it in their voice.
Yes, definitely, it has to be in their voice, their customers don't know who we are.
That also gives the notification service a clean rule. It never has to guess. Fresh ETA, send the window. Stale ETA, send the fallback. That's easy to test.

That's a good framing. It also makes it easier to justify in planning.
Works for me. I can own it. I think it's about a week for the backend part, and then the driver app change is small, I'd need someone from mobile for a day or two.

Well, it was the right line. That runbook is the best thing that happened on Thursday.
And the swarm was good. I think we had four engineers in the channel within ten minutes of the page, and nobody was stepping on each other. Kenji ruling out the model early saved us a rabbit hole.

And for what it's worth, once I did have something, the response from engineering was really quick. When I asked Maya what I could say, I had an answer in like two minutes. It's the before that was the problem.

Okay. Good. So, follow-ups, with names and rough dates. I'll read them off and then people can push back. Daniel, retry budgets with exponential backoff and jitter in the dispatch workers, and that includes not re-queuing the whole job on a single call failure.

Yep. I can have a PR up next week. I'd say rolled out by October ninth. And I'll also flip on periodic topology refresh in the Redis client config, everywhere, not just the ETA service. That's the ticket that's been sitting in the backlog since May, so, finally.

Love it. Then me. Circuit breaker on the ETA service, so it fails fast and serves degraded instead of crash-looping. Status page automation, so a sev-one alert sets the status page to investigating automatically, and ideally kicks off Sofia's comms flow at the same time. A monthly failover chaos test, where we deliberately fail over a Redis primary during business hours, low-traffic window, and watch what happens, staging first, then prod. And tightening the alert thresholds, plus a new alert on worker retry rate.
That's a lot on you, Ravi. Is that realistic?

The thresholds I'll do Monday, that's small. Status page automation is maybe two days. The breaker is the bigger one, I'd say two weeks. Chaos test, I'd like the first one in prod before the end of October. So, it's a lot, but it's doable if I'm not also pulled onto other stuff, which is your next point I think.
Sofia, customer comms runbook with pre-approved templates, and the named contact list for the big accounts.
Yes. I'll have a draft next week, before the Brightside QBR ideally, so I can actually tell Jordan it exists. Ravi, Daniel, I'll send you the templates for the technical review.
Kenji, staleness flag, which we just covered. And Maya.

Yeah. So mine is less of a ticket and more of a commitment. Q4 planning is next Friday, and I'm going to protect capacity for this. Everything Ravi just listed, plus Daniel's work, plus Kenji's flag, that's real engineering time, and it's competing with Routing v3 GA on November seventeenth, and with live ETA sharing, and with the driver onboarding stuff. And I think the honest thing to say is, if we don't explicitly ring-fence it, it'll get eaten. Exactly like the topology refresh ticket from May. So I'm going to propose we hold roughly twenty percent of routing and platform capacity for reliability work through Q4. And probably a change freeze on the dispatch path around Thanksgiving week, because that's peak for most of our grocery fleets.
I'll back that in planning. I'd rather slip something visible by a week than have a repeat of Thursday in Thanksgiving week. Brightside alone, that would be the renewal.
Okay. Good, I'll want you in that conversation.

And for the Brightside QBR on Wednesday, Jordan's going to ask about live ETA again. He asked in June. What I'd like to do is not promise a date on that call, because we haven't done planning, but promise that he gets a dated roadmap shortly after. Does that seem okay to everyone?
Yeah, please don't give him a date before Friday. Give him a date for when he'll get a date.
On the chaos test, Ravi, do you want help with the first one? I've done it in staging, I know where it's going to hurt.

Yes, please. I'd love that. My thinking is, the first time, we do staging, with the new retry budgets and topology refresh in, so we're testing the fixes, not just reproducing Thursday. Then the first prod one late October, a Tuesday around two p.m. Pacific, lowest-traffic window we have. And we announce it internally so nobody panics. Then it's on the calendar monthly.
Sounds right. And if the prod one goes badly, at least it goes badly on our schedule.
And last thing, I'll get the written postmortem cleaned up and published Monday, so Sofia has something to hand to customers.
That'd be amazing. I'll make a customer-facing version from it.
Okay. Anything I missed? Anyone want to push back on an owner or a date?
Okay. Thanks, everyone. Seriously. Not a fun one, but I think we know exactly what to fix. Go have a weekend.
notes: Blameless but honest retro on the Sep 24 ETA service outage. Covered the timeline, root cause, detection and comms, customer impact, and follow-ups with owners.

The failover was routine. What made it a 47-minute outage was having none of these three safeguards: Redis client topology refresh, worker retry budgets with jitter, and an ETA service circuit breaker. Any one of them would have shrunk it.
The topology refresh fix was already in Daniel's runbook from a May staging failover, but the prod ticket sat in the backlog with nothing forcing it.
Detection was slow. The page came 6 minutes after the storm began because of a 10%-for-5-minutes threshold, and the status page was manual and went up after 26 minutes.
The model service was healthy throughout. The customer-facing harm came from stale cached ETAs that nothing marked as stale.
Maya will ring-fence about 20% of routing and platform capacity for reliability work in Q4 so these fixes don't get deprioritized again.

From 14:20 to about 14:26, Ravi chased a harmless 13:50 logging deploy. The Redis dashboard looked healthy, and only the ETA service client logs showed the stale primary.
A pod-only restart at 14:41 fell over again by 14:43 because workers were still retrying, which cost about 10 minutes.
The Redis client had periodic topology refresh off by default, so it kept hitting the old primary until the process restarted.
About 1,800 dispatch workers retried in lockstep (fixed 200 ms, 5 attempts, then a full job re-queue) and multiplied ETA service load about 6x in 90 seconds.
The ETA service had no circuit breaker, so it exhausted its connection pool and crash-looped instead of degrading.
The status page was manual, and Ravi was both incident commander and debugging. Going forward, a sev-1 alert should set the page to 'investigating' automatically.
Sofia first heard about the outage from Brightside's Aisha around 14:22, while the status page was still green.
Sofia needs a comms runbook with pre-approved templates. Mid-incident she lost 15 minutes wordsmithing and checking what she was allowed to say.
The driver app kept counting down from its last ETA, and the notification service kept texting windows from a snapshot table that stopped updating at 14:14.
Kenji's staleness flag: expose a computed-at time on every ETA, with a default 5-minute threshold configurable per fleet. Show 'ETA updating' in the driver app and send a fallback customer message.
Asher framed the flag as a prerequisite for live ETA sharing.
Daniel: retry budgets with jitter and topology refresh everywhere by Oct 9.

Engineering answered Sofia's comms questions within about 2 minutes once she asked.
No retry budget or jitter in the dispatch workers, plus full job re-queues on a single failed call, so retries were retried again.

The status page was manual and 26 minutes late. The incident commander was also debugging, and secondary on-call was never paged.

turns: Hey. Hi. Okay, Tom's here. Asher, you're, I think you're on mute.

Exactly. So here's the funnel. This is from the last ninety days, all fleets. Install to account created, we lose about nine points. That's the email and password step. And then the big one. Seventeen on just the permission prompt? Wow.

Yeah. And it makes sense when you look at what we do today. We basically throw the OS prompt at them cold. Right after login, boom, allow Tandem to use your location, and on iOS we're asking for always, which, you know, iOS doesn't even let you ask for always directly anymore. So they get while using the app first, and then later this second prompt pops up in the middle of a route asking to upgrade to always, and people panic and hit don't allow. And then background tracking doesn't work, ETAs go stale for that driver, the dispatcher calls them, it's a mess.
That matches what I hear, honestly. Brightside's dispatchers call it the ghost driver thing. The driver's out on the road but the map shows them sitting at the depot for an hour.
Ghost driver. That's good, I'm stealing that.
And on Android it's not better, right? Background location is its own settings page.

Like, a driver who's never used routing software, why would you let a random app track you all the time? From their point of view that's creepy. What's the login drop about? Nine points on email and password feels high.
