Okay, the flow. So, screen one. This is the big change. No more email and password. You log in with your phone number, we text you a six-digit code, you type it in, you're in. The fleet already has the driver's phone number in most cases because dispatch uses it, so the invite is just a text with a link. Tap the link, it opens the app or the store, and the number's prefilled.
And the code autofills? Because typing six digits with gloves on, that's another drop-off.
Yes, on both platforms, it reads it from the SMS. And then we keep them logged in for, I think we said ninety days, unless the fleet revokes them. So no more morning password ritual. No notebook.
What about shared devices? I know some fleets have like a pool of phones that live in the vans.

Yeah, so that's the edge case. For shared devices the fleet can turn on a switch-driver option, and you log in with your number and the code each shift. It's still way faster than a password. It's maybe, I don't know, five percent of fleets that do shared devices.
Brightside doesn't, for what it's worth. Everyone uses their own phone and they get a stipend.

Okay, good. So, screen two through four. This is the permissions primer. Three steps, one per permission, and each one explains why before we ever show the OS prompt. So step one is location. And the copy is, roughly, your dispatcher and your customers see where you are so they get accurate delivery times, and we only track you while you're on shift. Then there's a little animation of the dot moving along a route and the ETA updating. And then a button that says allow location, and only then do we fire the system prompt. And on iOS we then immediately walk them through the always upgrade with a picture of exactly which option to tap.
Is it true, though? The only on shift part.
It is. Maya, correct me, but we stop the location updates when the route is completed or the driver goes off shift.

Yeah, that's right. We stop publishing. The OS permission is still always, technically, but we're not collecting anything off shift. I'd want legal to look at the exact wording, but the substance is true.

Good, I'll send it to legal. Step two is notifications. Why: your dispatcher can send you route changes and new stops without calling you while you drive. Short. And step three is camera, for proof of delivery photos and scanning barcodes. And camera, we actually ask at the moment you first need it on the practice route, not up front, because it tested better that way.
Tested where? Like with real drivers?

Six drivers. So small. Four from Brightside, two from the Columbus parcel fleet. Sofia set it up. Every one of them got through the location step on the first try in the new flow, and in the current flow, three of the six denied it. Which, it's six people, I'm not going to put that in a board deck, but it's the direction.
One of them said, and I wrote it down, oh, so that's why it wants that. Like it had never occurred to him.

Yeah, that was the moment for me. Okay, and then the last part, the practice route. This is the one that's going to be the most debate, I think. So after permissions, instead of dropping them into an empty home screen waiting for dispatch to assign something, we give them a practice route. It's three to five stops, it's fake, it's in a sandbox, nothing goes to the dispatcher or the customer. And it walks them through the actual mechanics. Start route, navigate to the stop, arrive, scan the package, take the proof of delivery photo, which is where we ask for the camera, mark it delivered, handle a failed delivery, like customer not home. And at the end it says you're ready, and the fleet sees in the dashboard that the driver completed practice.
About four minutes in testing. Maybe five if someone reads everything.
Okay. That's not bad. I was worried you'd say fifteen.

No, I'm very aware that every minute we add is a minute for them to drop off. But the theory is, the first real route is terrifying, there's a dispatcher watching, there's a van full of groceries, and right now the first time they ever see the scan screen is in front of a customer's door. So we're moving the learning to somewhere safe.
Aisha's basically doing a manual version of this today, for what it's worth. New drivers ride along with a depot lead for half a day before they get their own van.
Which is exactly the thing I'd love to replace with four minutes. Or at least make the half day a lot less painful.
When you say sandbox, what's actually generating the route? Because that's the part where my ears perked up.
I was hoping you'd ask that. Can we come back to it? Because I think it's tied to the skip question, and I want to do those together.
Sure. Yeah. But I'm going to come back to it.
Okay. So, the skip question. Should experienced drivers be able to skip the practice route? Right now the prototype has no skip. Everyone does it. And I go back and forth, honestly.

My instinct is yes, let them skip. If someone's been driving parcel for ten years and switched from another routing app, making them do a fake route feels kind of patronizing. And it's four minutes of friction right at the point where we're trying to remove friction.
Can I jump in? Because this is literally what I was talking to Aisha about before this call.

So Aisha's the fleet manager at Brightside, she runs the depots day to day. And they're about to hire their seasonal drivers for the holidays, November, December. She said, and I'm quoting her pretty closely, the seasonal drivers need it the most and they're also the ones who'll tell you they don't. Because everyone says they've driven delivery before. Some of them did, for like two weeks, three years ago, for a totally different company with a totally different app. And then on day one they don't know how to mark a failed delivery, and they call the depot lead, and the depot lead is dealing with twenty of them at once.
And she said, if you give them a skip button, they will all press it. Like, every single one. Her words were, they'll press skip faster than they press accept on the permissions.
Which, to be fair, is also a data point about the permissions.
Ha, yeah. But her point was, the experienced ones aren't her problem. Her problem is the fourteen people who start the week before Thanksgiving.
Could the fleet decide? Like a setting, require practice route, on or off.

I thought about that. I'm a bit wary of making it a setting, because then we have two flows to maintain and test, and the default matters way more than the setting. Most fleets never touch settings. Sofia, how many fleets have changed, like, any driver app setting?
Off the top of my head? Not many. Maybe a fifth. Maybe less.
Right. So whatever the default is, is basically the product.
What about a middle ground. You have to do at least one stop. Like the scan, the photo, mark delivered, the core loop. And then you can skip the rest.
Oh, I actually like that. Because the one stop is where all the real mechanics are. The other stops are mostly reinforcing, plus the failed delivery case.
I think Aisha would be okay with that. As long as they can't skip the whole thing. Honestly the failed delivery bit is the one she cares about though, the customer not home flow.
Then I can put the failed delivery in the first stop. Like stop one, the customer isn't home, you have to handle it. That's actually a more interesting first stop anyway.
Okay, now can I do my thing?

So, when I hear practice route in a sandbox, my worry is what that means on the backend. If the idea is we generate a real route around wherever the driver is standing, with real addresses near the depot, and we run it through the solver and the ETA service, then we're basically standing up a second copy of the routing stack that's isolated from production. Separate tenant, separate data, we'd have to make sure nothing leaks into the dispatcher view, into analytics, into billing, because we bill per active driver. That's not a design task, that's a quarter. And my team is pretty much all-in on v3 GA until November seventeenth.
Yeah. That's fair. In my head I didn't need it to be around where they're standing. That was just what the prototype faked.
Right, so that's the question. Does it need to be live? Like does the route need to be real, solved on the fly, with real ETAs, or can it just look real?
It can just look real. Honestly the driver doesn't care if the ETA is computed. They care that the screens are the real screens.

Then what I'd propose is we don't touch the solver at all. We take a few recorded routes, real ones from beta fleets, anonymized, scrub the addresses, and the app just replays them. The stops, the map, the ETAs, all prerecorded. The driver taps through the real UI, but nothing behind it is live. Like a flight simulator that only knows one airport.

Way smaller. I'm guessing, don't hold me to it, but the replay version is maybe two or three engineer-weeks, mostly on the app side, plus a little backend to serve the recorded routes and mark practice complete. The live version I wouldn't even estimate in this meeting. It's like ten weeks plus, and it touches everything we're trying to stabilize for GA.
And are we allowed to use beta customers' routes like that? Even scrubbed?

We'd strip the addresses and customer names entirely, it'd just be the stop geometry and timings. But yeah, I'd want to check the data terms. Or honestly we just use test routes we've recorded ourselves around Columbus.
Or I make one up. A fake neighborhood.
Made up is fine too, as long as it's a recorded file and not live.
Does a recorded route still work with the real map, though? Like if the driver is in Sacramento and the recorded route is in Columbus.
The map would just show Columbus. Or wherever. Does that matter?
I don't think drivers would care. Honestly it might be clearer. It's obviously practice, it's not your neighborhood.
Yeah, that's a good point. It also kills the risk that someone thinks it's a real delivery. Okay. I'm sold.

Okay, so let me say back what I think we've decided, and then there's two more things. One, drivers can skip the practice route, but only after completing one practice stop, and that first stop includes the failed delivery case. Two, the sandbox is built on recorded routes, no live solver, no live ETA service. Asher, are you comfortable calling those decided?

Yes. Both. On the first one, I came in wanting a full skip, and I think Aisha's point about seasonal drivers is just right. And on the second one, I'm not going to spend Maya's team on a second routing stack for a tutorial.
Great. Okay, the next thing is localization. Sofia, do you want to tee this up? It came from Brightside too.

Yeah. So, Aisha again, sorry, she's very opinionated, which is great. A big chunk of their drivers prefer Spanish. She said for the seasonal hires it's something like a third, maybe more in the Sacramento area if they expand there. And right now the app is English only. So the permissions primer, which is all about explaining why, is kind of useless if they can't read the why.
Is that just the onboarding flow or the whole app?

That's exactly the scope question. I think v1 is the onboarding flow plus the core route screens, the ones the practice route touches. Which, conveniently, is the same set. It's maybe two hundred strings. Not the settings, not the help center.
And we'd need someone to actually translate it well. Not just machine translation.
Yeah, we'd use a proper vendor, and I'd want a couple of Spanish-speaking drivers to review it. Sofia, could Aisha find two or three people?

From the engineering side, the app already has the string extraction set up, we just never shipped a second language. So adding Spanish to those screens is not big, it's mostly QA. Layout stuff, Spanish strings are longer, buttons wrap.
I'll design for the longer strings from the start. Okay. So, Asher, Spanish in v1?

Yes, Spanish in v1. Onboarding and the core route screens. If we're aiming for under fifteen percent drop-off and a third of grocery seasonal drivers can't read the screens, we're not going to hit fifteen anyway.
Okay, three decisions. Love it. And then the last thing, which is the one I can't solve. Who builds this?

So my rough sizing is: the app-side onboarding flow, login, primer, practice route UI, Spanish, that's the bulk of it, and it's mostly frontend and mobile. Plus Maya's two or three weeks for the replay backend. And right now we have, effectively, nobody on frontend who isn't already on something.
That's what the two Senior Frontend reqs are for. Hannah's got a few in the pipeline. Sam Rivera is the strongest, he's onsite next week, I think.

Right, but even if Sam says yes the day after his onsite, with notice, he's starting, what, early November? And then he needs a couple of weeks to ramp. So realistically mid-November before anyone's writing onboarding code. That's fine for a Q4 target if we're okay landing it in December, but that's tight.

And I'll just say the obvious thing. The other big frontend ask for Q4 is live ETA sharing. The tracking link. Harbor & Pine wants it as a must-have, Brightside's asked twice. That's about five engineer-weeks, and it's the same people. So whoever we hire, they're going to get pulled in two directions.
And Brightside wants both, for what it's worth. The tracking link is the thing Jordan asks about. Onboarding is the thing Aisha asks about.
Is there a version where onboarding ships in slices? Like phone login first, because it's the smallest and it kills the notebook, then the primer, then the practice route?
Maybe. That's a good thing to put in the sizing. Show me the slices and what each one buys us in drop-off.

But on onboarding versus live ETA, I don't want to decide that here, because it's the actual Q4 trade-off and it needs Tom and everyone in the room. That's what Q4 planning is for. What I'll do is bring both, sized, to planning. Priya, can you give me a real engineer-week number for onboarding, not a vibe?
And I'll check with Hannah on where Sam is and whether we can move faster on the second req.
And I'll write up the replay backend estimate properly, so it's not just me saying two or three weeks on a call.

Perfect. And in the meantime I'll update the prototype with the skip after one stop and the failed delivery first, and send the location copy to legal. And Sofia, if you can ask Aisha about the Spanish reviewers, and maybe whether we can test the new flow with a couple of her seasonal hires when they start.
On it. I'll ask her this week.
Okay. That's it, that was actually productive. Thank you all.
Really nice work, Priya. The primer especially.
Thanks, Priya. And thank you for not making me build a second solver.

turns: Okay, I think — is that everyone? I see Maya, Daniel, Priya. Kenji, hi. Ravi. Sofia's here. Tom's — Tom said he's two minutes out, he's coming off a call with Harbor & Pine, so let's just start and he can catch up.
Can you hear me okay? I switched headsets, this one's been kind of flaky.
You're good. A little quiet, but good.

Better. So, okay. Thanks everyone for doing this on a Friday afternoon, I know for some of you it's the last meeting of the week and you'd rather be anywhere else. The goal today is simple to say and hard to do. We have to leave this call with Q4 priorities that we actually believe in. Not a wish list. And the constraint is capacity. Maya and I went through it on Wednesday and it's about eleven engineers, call it eleven, for the quarter, and that's before holidays and on-call eat into it.

Eleven-ish. Eleven is generous, honestly. Once you take out on-call, Thanksgiving week, and the December freeze starting the 14th, it's more like nine and a half engineers of actual building time. And most of that is already spoken for by v3 GA. I'll get into the math when we hit the trade-offs, but I want everyone walking in knowing it's tight.

Which is exactly why we're doing this as one meeting and not five separate ones. So, the agenda. First, ten minutes or less on Q3, where we landed. Then Routing v3 GA scope, because that's the thing we've committed to and the date's not moving. Then the — the stuff that's competing for whatever's left. Live ETA sharing, driver onboarding, and Ravi's reliability follow-ups from the outage. Then we make the call, and then OKRs and owners. I'd like us to actually decide things today. If we walk out with 'let's take it offline' on everything, I've failed.
Hey, sorry, sorry — I'm here. What did I miss?
Nothing yet. You're right on time for the part where I say we're deciding things today.
Great. Love that. Love deciding things.
I say it every time, Sofia.

Okay, one ground rule. The docs are all in the folder — the capacity sheet, the beta report, Priya's onboarding funnel. I'm not going to screen-share all of them. If you need a number, ask, and whoever owns it answers. Cool? Okay. Maya, do you want to do the Q3 numbers or should I?

So, Q3. The headline is Routing v3 beta. We've had six fleets on it since September 8th, and the results are honestly better than I expected. Eleven percent fewer miles driven — that's across all six, weighted — and on-time delivery went from 91.2 to 94.6 percent. Which, for context, the target we set back in the spring was 93.
That's the slide. That's the slide I want in every deck.

And it's held up, which is the part I care about. It's not like week one was great and then it decayed. Week four was actually the best week. On the engineering side, quick scorecard. We shipped the solver migration, the beta rollout tooling, and the new dispatch board filters. What slipped was the CSV import rewrite, about three weeks, mostly because we pulled two people onto beta support when the second beta fleet had that whole depot geocoding mess. I'd make that trade again. But it's why I'm allergic to anything unplanned this quarter. Every time we've said it's just a couple of weeks this year, it's been double.
It has been double. I have the receipts.

One caveat, small one. The eleven percent is miles, not time. Drive-time savings are more like eight, eight and a half, because the solver is happy to take a slightly slower road if it saves distance. Nobody's complained. But if sales says 'eleven percent faster,' that's wrong.
Noted. Fewer miles, not faster. Got it.
And part of the on-time number is the ETA model. Mean absolute error went from 6.1 to 4.3 minutes on the beta fleets. I'll talk about where it's still bad later.

Yeah, let's save that for GA scope. And good catch, Daniel, on miles versus time. Okay, and then the not-great part of Q3. Ravi, can you do the short version of the 24th? Short version — we did the long version in the retro.

Yeah. So Thursday, September 24th, the ETA service was down for forty-seven minutes, 14:12 to 14:59 UTC. Root cause: the Redis cluster did a failover, which on its own should've been a blip, but the dispatch workers all retried at once — no backoff, no jitter — and that retry storm knocked the ETA service over. Three hundred and twelve fleets affected. Drivers saw stale ETAs and end customers got wrong delivery windows. And — I'll just say it — the status page was updated twenty-six minutes in. That's on us. That's on me, really.
It's on the process, not just you.
Sure, but right now I'm the process. Anyway. I've got follow-ups, I'll get to them in the reliability section.

Can I add the customer side for a second? Because Brightside was the loudest one. Jordan called me directly, which he doesn't do. Their drivers were staring at ETAs that were forty minutes old, and their customers got texts saying 'arriving 2:15' for orders that showed up at three-something. Groceries. Ice cream melting, the whole thing. And Aisha, their fleet manager, told me her dispatch team was refreshing our status page and it said 'all systems operational' for almost half an hour. That's the part that stung.

And — this matters for later — Jordan, on that same call, brought up live ETA sharing again. That's the second time he's asked. He said, more or less, 'if my customers could see where the van actually is, the outage would've been half as bad.' I don't know if that's true, but that's how he feels.
Okay, let's hold that, because that's like forty percent of today.
Holding it. Just flagging, renewal is January 31st and they're at a hundred and forty-five K.
Can I do pipeline real quick?

So, pipeline is strong. Genuinely — not sales-strong, actually strong. The big one, obviously, is Harbor & Pine. Four hundred and twenty trucks, regional freight in the Pacific Northwest. About three-ten ARR, which would be our biggest logo by a lot. Decision is October 30th. We're up against RouteWise, who are cheaper — I'll be honest, they're cheaper by a meaningful amount. Marcus Hill, their ops director, is our champion and he's great, he gets it. But the CFO, Dana Whitfield, is the one signing, and we've never been on a call with her.
Never. Marcus says she reads the summary and decides. So whatever Marcus brings her is what we've got.
And integrations? Last I heard, Elena had questions about the TMS.

Elena's fine. Well — Elena's fine-ish. They run Samsara for telematics, which is easy, we've done that a dozen times. And an old on-prem Oracle TMS, which is less easy. But she's not a blocker, she's just thorough.
Thorough is fine. Oracle on-prem is the part that eats a week.
Sure. Anyway — beyond Harbor & Pine we've got three mid-size grocery deals in late stage, and all three want v3. So GA landing on time matters for them too, not just for the OKR.

The two regional grocery chains in Texas, and the parcel fleet in Denver that did the pilot over the summer. Together they're about the same ARR as Harbor & Pine, give or take, but they're three separate signatures, so the risk is spread out. All three asked about v3 timing in the last two weeks. One of them asked about live tracking too, but casually. Not a must-have.

Okay. Good to know it's not just one deal holding up the quarter. Okay. So Q3 in one sentence: v3 works, the outage hurt us with exactly the customer we can't afford to hurt, and the pipeline is real but the biggest deal depends on someone we've never met.

Can I sneak one thing in? On the driver app side, Q3 was mostly research. We did the funnel analysis and nineteen interviews with new drivers. I'll show the numbers in the onboarding section, but the short version is the drop-off is worse than we thought it was.
I'll save it. It's a good reveal.
Okay, v3 GA. Daniel, you've got the scope doc. Walk us through it, and flag anything that's at risk.

Sure. So, GA is November 17th, that hasn't changed. What's in: the new solver becomes the default for every new fleet starting that day. Existing fleets get a migration wizard — they can opt in at GA, and we want everyone moved by end of January. Kenji's ETA model replaces the old heuristic ETAs for anyone on v3. Time windows and driver break rules, which the beta fleets have been using. And API parity with v2, which is the boring part that takes the longest, honestly, because there are like four endpoints that nobody documented and three customers depend on.
Two customers. We killed one of those dependencies last week.

Two. Even better. What's out of GA: multi-day routes and EV charging constraints. Both go to Q1, and I've already told the two beta fleets who asked about EV, so nobody's surprised. Code freeze for GA is November 10th. The rollout is staged — twenty-five percent of eligible fleets on the 17th, then fifty the week after, and everyone eligible by December 1st, before the holiday freeze. The migration wizard is the piece I'd watch. It's a lot of edge cases. Depots with weird geocodes, fleets with custom service times, that kind of thing.

And for staffing, GA is taking six of the eleven through November. Daniel's leading it, three on solver and API parity, Kenji on the model, and one floating between the migration wizard and beta support. I'm not moving anyone off that until we're past December 1st. That's the one thing I'm going to be stubborn about today.
That's fair. GA is the one we've told the board about.
And the beta fleets just — they stay on, right? They don't get flipped back or anything?
They stay on. They're basically already GA, they just don't know it.
Love that. Can I put 'eleven percent fewer miles' on the website yet? Leah's been asking me for a case study from one of the beta fleets, and I keep telling her to wait.
Talk to Leah offline. Use one fleet that's agreed to be named, and use Daniel's wording — miles, not time.
And please not the fleet with the depot geocoding problem. Their first two weeks were a mess.
Two things. API parity, which I just said, and that's a known amount of grind, I'm not worried about it. The real one is the ETA model in certain conditions. Kenji should explain it, it's his.

Okay. So the 4.3 minute number is real, but it's an average across everything. When I break it down by stop type, it's very uneven. Suburban residential, it's under four minutes, it's good. Dense urban stops — downtown, apartment buildings, places where parking takes longer than the drive — the error is about 8.9 minutes. And loading docks are worse. If there's a dock wait, the error is around twelve minutes, and the tail is long. Some stops are off by thirty.

On some stops. Not many. The problem is we don't observe the dock wait. The driver arrives, the truck sits, and we only see that it left later. So the model has nothing to learn from. For urban, I built a mode that uses dwell-time priors by building type and time of day. It helps. In the two beta fleets that are mostly urban, it brings the error down to around six. But it's only tested on those two fleets.
So the question is whether urban-dense mode is in GA or not.
Can I — sorry, just to be the sales guy for a second. Harbor & Pine is basically all loading docks. Regional freight. Every stop is a dock.
Okay. That's — okay. Good to know before Marcus finds out on his own.

Which, to be clear, we tell them. If Marcus asks how accurate our ETAs are, the honest answer is 4.3 minutes on average, and docks are the hardest case, and that's exactly where their data would help. That's a better answer than pretending.
